newsitem.title: UK: Major says he can win election but admits mistakes.
newsitem.headline: Major says he can win election but admits mistakes.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major believes voters will return to the banner of his Conservatives and he can still win Britain's looming general election despite trailing the opposition Labour party badly in opinion polls.

But he also told a television interviewer late on Wednesday he had made mistakes, in particular the decision to shepherd Britain into the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) in 1990 only to crash out two years later.
Major, whose loss last week of a by-election with a swing to Labour of 17 points pushed him into a parliamentary minority, said: "I believe opinion will change and I believe I will win.
"I'm not complacent about that. There's a huge amount to be done. But I certainly believe we can win this election."
Major told a BBC interviewer that the state of the economy, and the tough decisions the government had been forced to take, was what would bring voters back to his party.
Saying Britain's prospects were brighter than anyone could remember, he said: "That can't wholly be luck. It must have something to do with the decisions we've taken, and it is.

"Some of the decisions we have taken have been very unpopular indeed and we have been bitterly attacked for them. But, self-evidently, from what is happening in the economy, they were right decisions."
Major admitted that it had been a political mistake to take Britain into the ERM, which the country was forced out of after markets attacked the pound in September 1992.
But he said participation in the ERM, which Britain joined in 1990 when he was prime minister Margaret Thatcher's finance minister, had helped to prevent high inflation.
"Going into the ERM is seen by many people as a mistake... Politically it can certainly be said to have been a mistake.

"But economically, if we had not gone into the Exchange Rate Mechanism I very much doubt we would have killed inflation as comprehensively as we had. But we came out of it in ignominious circumstances and that was a political mistake," Major said.
Britain joined the ERM in October 1990, locking sterling in at a high exchange rate which crushed the domestic economy.

Britain's exit two years later allowed interest rates to be cut and the pound to fall, making British exports more competitive in overseas markets and Britain the fastest growing major economy in Europe in recent years.
But Thatcher blamed Major in her memoirs for arguing in favour of entry into the ERM against her wishes when he was her Chancellor of the Exchequer.

Many commentators also trace voters' reluctance to reward Major for the country's buoyant economy back to "Black Wednesday", the day the pound was forced out of the ERM, damaging the government's reputation for economic competence.

Major said on Wednesday: "Everybody believed at the time -- the Tory (Conservative) Party, Labour Party, Liberal Party, City -- that we should go into the Exchange Rate Mechanism. Events made a monkey of us...It's the area that's had the biggest blot on what subsequently happened in the eyes of the public."
Major has moved sharply to the right on Europe since 1992 under pressure from Conservative Eurosceptics in his party who want Britain to loosen links with Brussels.
But in the interview, Major sought to hold a steady line on the single currency, despite recent rows over cabinet ministers appearing to harden policy against British entry.
He said there were advantages to a single currency, but he would only take Britain in if it was in the national interest.
Major also repeated scepticism that the scheme would start on time in 1999, saying he did not believe many European states would meet the stringent economic criteria for entry.
